home.heroTitle:
Wagyu, one slice
at a time.
home.heroLead: Japanese Kuroge Wagyu sukiyaki and shabu-shabu, cooked at your table.
home.introTitle: From choosing the beef to the last slice
introBody: Every day we select the best Kuroge Wagyu available and cut each part to the thickness that suits it.
For sukiyaki, our staff cook your first slice and show you when it is ready. No experience needed. Just come hungry.
home.stylesLead: Same Wagyu, two very different meals. If you can only choose one, start with sukiyaki.

sukiyaki.name: Sukiyaki
sukiyaki.body: Beef seared in a cast-iron pot with sweet soy sauce, then dipped in beaten egg. The richest way to taste Wagyu fat.

shabushabu.name: Shabu-shabu
shabushabu.body: Thin slices swished for a few seconds in kombu broth, then dipped in sesame sauce or citrus ponzu. Light, clean, and tender.

home.firstBody: Why raw egg? How long do you swish the beef? Our step-by-step guide has you covered.
galleryAlt: Wagyu cooking in a cast-iron pot
home.conceptTitle: From choosing the beef to the last slice
home.banquetBody: From private rooms for two to a hall for up to 24 guests. Ideal for business dinners, celebrations, and family gatherings.

menu.title: Menu

menu.note: Courses may change with seasonal availability. Please tell us about any allergies when you book.

guide.title: How to eat
guide.lead: Our staff will help you at the table, so there is nothing to memorize. Knowing the flow just makes it more fun.

sukiyakiSteps.title: Beat the egg
sukiyakiSteps.body: Lightly beat the raw egg in your small bowl. Dipping the hot beef cools it slightly and makes it silky. Eggs in Japan are produced to be eaten raw.

sukiyakiSteps.title: We cook the first slice
sukiyakiSteps.body: Your server sears the first slice in the sauce and serves it at its best, so you can see how it should look.

sukiyakiSteps.title: Beef first, then vegetables
sukiyakiSteps.body: Simmer vegetables and tofu in the sauce once it has taken on the flavor of the beef.

sukiyakiSteps.title: Finish with rice
sukiyakiSteps.body: Pour the remaining sauce and egg over rice to end the meal.

shabuSteps.title: Heat the broth
shabuSteps.body: When the kombu broth is at a gentle simmer, you are ready.

shabuSteps.title: Swish a few times
shabuSteps.body: Hold one slice with chopsticks and swish it through the broth 2–3 times. It is ready when a little pink remains.

shabuSteps.title: Dip in sauce
shabuSteps.body: Rich sesame sauce or light citrus ponzu. Try both.

shabuSteps.title: Finish with porridge or udon
shabuSteps.body: We use the flavorful broth to make rice porridge or udon noodles.

guide.eggTitle: Prefer not to eat raw egg?
guide.eggBody: We can serve a soft-boiled egg, or sukiyaki without egg. Just ask.
